headline: Connecticut prepares HUSKY D enrollees for Medicaid work rules starting Jan. 1
dek: State officials are promoting outreach and eligibility tools as new federal requirements threaten coverage for roughly 108,000 HUSKY D enrollees who do not document work, training, education or an exemption.
body: Connecticut officials are trying to keep residents connected to HUSKY D as new federal Medicaid requirements approach, but the state has not committed to replacing federal money that could be lost. Gov. Ned Lamont and state health officials gathered at Stamford Hospital on Monday to explain the outreach effort ahead of rules that begin Jan. 1. The event and the governor's position were reported by [CT Mirror](https://ctmirror.org/2026/10/05/lamont-ct-response-to-medicaid-cuts/), while [WFSB](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/05/state-leaders-detail-plans-support-husky-health-d-recipients-ahead-new-rules/?outputType=amp) previewed the state's plan and the timing of the announcement.

The change applies to HUSKY D, Connecticut's Medicaid coverage for low-income adults without dependent children. CT Mirror reported that Andrea Barton Reeves, commissioner of the Department of Social Services, said the new federal law puts coverage for about 108,000 HUSKY D residents at risk. That figure describes people who could be affected by the new rules; it does not mean all 108,000 will lose coverage. Eligibility will depend on each person's work, income, education, community-service activity and qualifying exemptions.

Under the Connecticut Department of Social Services' [official H.R.1 guidance](https://portal.ct.gov/dss/all-programs/dss-benefits-and-hr1/hr1-for-members/hr1-work-rule-changes), an affected adult can satisfy the new rule by earning at least $580 a month, working at least 80 hours a month, completing at least 80 hours of community service, or taking part in an approved work or training program for at least 80 hours. Enrollment at least half-time in an education program can also qualify. The guidance says combinations of qualifying activities may be used to reach 80 hours, so the rule is broader than a simple requirement to hold a conventional job.

The same DSS page lists categories that are exempt, including parents or caregiver relatives of a child under 14, pregnant or postpartum people, foster and former foster youth, American Indian or Alaska Native people, certain veterans, and people who are medically frail. People recently released from jail or prison, people in drug or alcohol treatment, and some people experiencing a short-term hardship may also qualify for an exemption. The exemptions matter because a missed work-hour target does not by itself establish that someone is ineligible for HUSKY D; the agency must apply the full eligibility rules to the person's circumstances.

DSS says it is building ways to confirm eligibility from records the state already has, a process commonly called ex parte verification. CT Mirror reported that the department is using that approach to reduce the paperwork required from people whose information already demonstrates that they qualify. The state has also launched [MedicaidMattersCT.org](https://www.medicaidmattersct.org/) as an information resource. DSS's H.R.1 materials direct residents to community action agencies for help understanding the new work rules and reporting qualifying hours.

The policy debate is also about money. Connecticut has used $115 million from an emergency response fund to help offset the expiration of federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans, according to CT Mirror. Lamont said the state would first concentrate on helping eligible residents use the benefits that remain available and did not promise state dollars to replace the Medicaid cuts. That leaves an unresolved question for lawmakers and the administration: whether Connecticut will later spend state money to protect coverage for people who are eligible under current state rules but cannot meet the new federal conditions.

For Stamford, Monday's event put the national Medicaid changes in a local setting. The gathering included Stamford Mayor Caroline Simmons, Stamford Health officials and city health-and-human-services staff, according to WFSB. Their role is primarily outreach: helping residents understand what will change, who may be exempt and what documents they may need. The event did not change the federal effective date or create a new coverage category.

The immediate deadline is Jan. 1, 2027, when the work and community-engagement rules take effect. The DSS FAQ also says HUSKY D adults will renew every six months instead of every 12 months beginning Jan. 1, and applicants will face a shorter period of retroactive coverage. Residents who rely on HUSKY D should use the official DSS guidance, respond to renewal notices and seek help from a community action agency before assuming that a new rule ends their coverage. The practical outcome will depend on how the state verifies exemptions, counts qualifying activity and handles people whose circumstances change during the transition.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Connecticut HUSKY D Medicaid work rules begin Jan. 1
seoDescription: Connecticut is preparing HUSKY D enrollees for new Medicaid work and community-engagement rules that begin Jan. 1, 2027.
